title: Nasdaq drops 5.3% as AI selloff deepens on Anthropic's first full trading day
subtitle: Anthropic shares fell 8.5% to close at $88.91 — just above the $83 IPO price — while the Nasdaq Composite erased its 2026 gains and Nvidia fell 14%.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% on Friday, its worst session in more than two years, erasing the index's gains for 2026 and pushing the S&P 500 — down 3.7% — into correction territory alongside it, per CNBC, CNN and Axios. Anthropic's stock dropped 8.5% to close at $88.91 on its first full trading day as a public company, just above the $83 IPO price. The IPO had been expected to steady the AI trade; instead Anthropic opened Thursday at $111.50, closed Thursday at $97.17, and surrendered another chunk on Friday. Nvidia shares fell nearly 14% in the same session on the SEC accounting probe disclosure.

The proximate causes are familiar — SEC scrutiny of Nvidia's accounting, tightening credit, the Commerce Department chip-sale disclosures, the midterms' decisive ballot results against data-center expansion — but the signal worth watching is correlation. In 2025, hyperscaler and chipmaker drawdowns were absorbed by neighboring AI positions. On Friday, the correlation ran the other way. CoreWeave, Oracle, Palantir, AMD and Broadcom all fell with Nvidia. Anthropic, two days post-IPO, could not decouple from its own supplier ecosystem. That is what a regime change in the AI trade looks like: the names move together on the way down, not just on the way up.

Analysts are not calling it a bubble burst yet. The CNBC piece quotes strategists describing it as a reset in valuations that had priced AI capex growth as a secular constant. Anthropic's $81 billion raise — the largest IPO in history by proceeds — now sits on a balance sheet that will be expected to defend the Mythos and Fable roadmap, the $26 billion separate placement that closed alongside the offering, and compute commitments disclosed in the S-1 that run through 2028. The stock's immediate behavior tells you what public-market discipline looks like: it does not wait for the next model release.

A note for learners: 'correction' is a technical label, not a diagnosis. The useful question after a session like Friday is which line items in the AI capex cycle are actually cash-backed and which depend on circular financing. Nvidia disclosed on Tuesday it would be 'far more selective' about AI financing deals. Hyperscaler capex guidance is still rising. Both can be true at once, and the resolution shows up in the data center bookings and the contract durations — not in the day-to-day tape.
